source: Krieglstein et al. (2022) Systematic meta-analysis of the reliability and validity of subjective cognitive load questionnaires in experimental multimedia learning research -- sample
finding: Meta-analysis of four common load questionnaires (Leppink 2013 and 2014, Klepsch 2017, Eysink 2009). The pool is mostly university students in multimedia experiments.
numbers: 53 articles, 67 experiments, N=7413. Mean age 20.4, 63.5% women. Mean sample 103.3 (SD 68.0). Authors had to email for correlation matrices; studies without data were dropped.
limits: Only experimental multimedia studies in English. Missing-data exclusions may bias the pool. Leppink 2014 and Eysink 2009 rest on few effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Subjective load scales are well studied but narrow: young students, multimedia. Do not assume they transfer to other systems.

source: Krieglstein et al. (2022) Systematic meta-analysis of the reliability and validity of subjective cognitive load questionnaires in experimental multimedia learning research -- reliability
finding: Internal consistency was satisfactory for all instruments. Moderators: age, education, domain and presentation mode did not change reliability, but the number of scale points did (odd-point and 9-point scales did well; even-point scales were worse).
numbers: Pooled Cronbach alpha for Leppink 2013: ICL .776, ECL .798, GCL .734 (ECL and ICL above GCL). Leppink 2014: ICL .851, ECL .788, GCL .806. Eysink 2009 ECL .740. Authors favour a 9-point scale. Rank tests show no sign of publication bias.
limits: Alpha measures consistency, not validity. High alpha can come from overlapping item wording.
agent_relevance: Reliability is not the weak spot of self-ratings; validity is.

source: Krieglstein et al. (2022) Systematic meta-analysis of the reliability and validity of subjective cognitive load questionnaires in experimental multimedia learning research -- construct validity of the three load types
finding: Load types correlate in ways that partly contradict theory. Intrinsic and extraneous load correlate positively. Extraneous and germane load correlate negatively in most questionnaires. The authors still say results lean toward the three-factor model.
numbers: Leppink 2013: ICL-ECL r+=.298 (k=25, 95% CI .221 to .370). Largest negative ECL-GCL r+=-.33 (Leppink 2014). In Eysink 2009 all three types correlate positively. The table text was garbled in the PDF extract, so only these two values were checked by hand.
limits: Correlations between types do not match theory. Hard to settle from correlations alone.
agent_relevance: Splitting load into intrinsic, extraneous and germane by questionnaire is unreliable. The agent should track one crude load signal, not three.

source: Krieglstein et al. (2022) Systematic meta-analysis of the reliability and validity of subjective cognitive load questionnaires in experimental multimedia learning research -- criterion validity
finding: Correlations of load ratings with learning are small and in the direction theory predicts, but germane ratings are weak predictors. Higher ICL and ECL go with worse retention and transfer; higher GCL with better.
numbers: Leppink 2013: ICL-retention r+=-.061 (CI -.140 to .019, ns), ECL-retention -.114, GCL-retention .188 (k=15), ICL-transfer -.188, ECL-transfer -.120, GCL-transfer .173. Klepsch 2017: ECL-transfer -.261, GCL-transfer .217. Eysink 2009: GCL correlates NEGATIVELY with retention (-.223) and transfer (-.182). Ratings also fall with prior knowledge.
limits: Effects are r about .1 to .26. The authors call the GCL link surprisingly low. Eysink GCL items judged poorly worded.
agent_relevance: Self-rated load explains a few percent of learning variance at most. Task accuracy is the better signal for the agent.

source: Ayres, Lee, Paas and van Merrienboer (2021) The validity of physiological measures to identify differences in intrinsic cognitive load -- design and overall result
finding: Systematic review (vote count, not an effect-size meta-analysis) of 2016-2020 studies that varied intrinsic load. It asked whether each measure showed a difference and whether it matched the expected difference. Nearly all measures had some validity, but sensitivity varied a lot.
numbers: 208 records screened, 98 after abstracts, 28 studies and 33 experiments. Mean 29.2 participants per experiment (SD 14.8). Detection rate: subjective 94% (30/32), eyes 87% (20/23), skin 85% (11/13), heart 68% (15/22), brain 68% (23/34). Kruskal-Wallis on detection chi2=9.67, df=4, p=.046; no pairwise difference survived Benjamini-Hochberg.
quote: nearly all the physiological measures identified in this sample had some level of validity
limits: Intrinsic load only, young adults, Web of Science only, small n per measure. No effect sizes or self-report correlations reported.
agent_relevance: Different measures disagree even on simple load manipulations. Use more than one signal (tokens and accuracy), not one proxy.

source: Ayres, Lee, Paas and van Merrienboer (2021) The validity of physiological measures to identify differences in intrinsic cognitive load -- which measures matched
finding: Match to the expected load ordering separates the measures. Subjective and eye measures match well, brain measures poorly. Single-item ratings did best.
numbers: Match rate: subjective 78%, eyes 78%, heart 64%, skin 62%, brain 32% (chi2=18.52, p<.001). Single-item ratings 100% detection and 100% match (8 instances). NASA-demand 100% / 86%; NASA-overall 90% / 70%; NASA-effort 86% / 57%. Blink rate 100% / 83%; pupil diameter 73% / 64%. EEG beta 71% / 0%; theta 50% / 17%; heart-rate variability 50% / 50%. Mean deviation from expected: subjective -0.19, eyes -0.30, brain -1.15.
limits: Counts, not effect sizes. Stress confounds possible in surgery simulations. Blood pressure and skin temperature rest on 3 studies.
agent_relevance: A cheap one-item rating beat expensive physiology. Supports a simple scalar (token count) over a complex instrument.

source: Ayres, Lee, Paas and van Merrienboer (2021) The validity of physiological measures to identify differences in intrinsic cognitive load -- task-type moderator
finding: Validity depends on task type. Memory tasks gave the best agreement; simulations, shape and word tasks were worse, and heart measures failed on word tasks.
numbers: Memory tasks 90% detection and 90% match. Arithmetic tasks 90% detection, 65% match. Heart measures on word tasks 0%.
limits: Few studies per task class. Task type is confounded with measure type.
agent_relevance: A load measure validated on one task class may fail on another. Check any token-based load rule per task type.

source: Jiang and Kalyuga (2020) Confirmatory factor analysis of cognitive load ratings supports a two-factor model
finding: A twelve-item rating questionnaire (adapted from Leppink 2013) fits a two-factor model (intrinsic plus extraneous) well when the germane items are treated as extra intrinsic items with reversed scoring. This supports the view that germane load is not a separate measurable thing.
numbers: N=60 first-year EFL students in China, listening lesson. Chi2=54.069, df=53, p=.433; CFI .994; TLI .993; RMSEA .018; SRMR .077. Cronbach alpha .78. All loadings above .30 except CL11 (.28).
quote: The results of the analysis supported the two-factor model of cognitive load.
limits: Small N (60) is a stated limit. Only the two-factor model was tested, with no head-to-head against a three-factor model. Data from one earlier experiment, one domain. Reverse-coding germane items is the authors' choice.
agent_relevance: Rival theory to the three-load view. Model load as two parts at most (task difficulty and wasted effort), not three.

source: Jiang and Kalyuga (2020) -- background: partial replications of the 3-factor scale
finding: Background in the paper: Leppink 2013 validated the 10-item scale in four experiments. Experiments 2 and 4 only partly supported three factors, and germane ratings did not correlate significantly with performance. Leppink 2014 later said support for the third factor as germane load was limited. Gerjets 2006 modified NASA-TLX items for the three loads without conclusive evidence.
numbers: Leppink 2013: PCA (Exp 1) and EFA (Exp 3) supported 3 factors; Exp 2 and 4 only partially.
limits: Reported second-hand from the paper's introduction.
agent_relevance: Partial replications of the three-factor structure were already visible in the original validation work.

source: Schuessler et al. (2024) Investigating construct validity of cognitive load measurement using single-item subjective rating scales
finding: Single-item scales for invested mental effort and perceived task difficulty track relative task difficulty and task demands, but they are not the same measure. Ratings related more to difficulty for open-ended items (no answer options) than for multiple choice, and delayed ratings follow the harder items in a set.
numbers: Chemistry test, N=1543 students, mean age 15.2, 128 items in 32 tasks. Perceived task difficulty vs relative item difficulty: r=-.80 for open-ended items (n=65) vs r=-.45 for multiple choice (n=61); Cohen q=.62, z=3.41. R2 .643 vs .199. Effort vs perceived difficulty r=.78; effort vs relative difficulty r=-.69 (32 tasks). Open items harder than multiple-choice, d=.38. Integrating items harder than selecting (p=.004).
limits: Ratings are at task level (4 items), so item-level claims are inferred. German school chemistry only.
agent_relevance: Difficulty and effort ratings differ, so the choice of rating matters. Open-ended generation raises load in a way answer options hide.

source: David, Biwer, Baars, Wijnia, Paas and de Bruin (2024) The relation between perceived mental effort, monitoring judgments, and learning outcomes: a meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analytic structural equation model. Perceived mental effort has only a small indirect link to learning, running through confidence judgments. Learners use effort as a cue for how well they learned. The direct effort-to-learning path was not significant.
numbers: 35 papers, 83 independent samples, 236 effect sizes. Full mediation model: effort to monitoring beta=-.19 (95% CI -.27 to -.12); monitoring to learning beta=.29 (CI .22 to .36); indirect effect beta=-.05 (CI -.08 to -.03). Partial model direct effort to learning beta=-.07 (CI -.16 to .02), ns. Moderators (education, effort wording, task type, difficulty) all non-significant.
limits: Few studies per moderator level, so moderator nulls are weak. Partial model was saturated. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Self-rated effort is a metacognitive cue, not a readout of load. Expect the same for model-stated confidence or effort. Prefer measured tokens and accuracy.

source: Scheiter, Ackerman and Hoogerheide (2020) Looking at mental effort appraisals through a metacognitive lens: are they biased?
finding: Review: subjective and most objective effort measures are each sensitive to task complexity, but little is known about whether they agree with each other. Several studies show dissociations, and people use heuristic cues (such as response time) when rating effort.
numbers: Paas 1994: heart-rate variability separated only active from rest, while effort ratings tracked task design. Antonenko and Niederhauser 2010: EEG showed less effort with hypertext leads, ratings did not. Korbach 2017 (seductive details): difficulty ratings linked to lower performance, effort ratings and pupil dilation unrelated to learning. Richter and Scheiter 2019: pupil size showed the signalling benefit for low-prior-knowledge learners, ratings did not. Nourbakhsh 2017: skin response classified 4 load levels up to 80% accuracy; Haapalainen 2010 and Larmuseau 2019 found no EDA difference.
limits: Narrative review; no pooled effect sizes. Dual-task measures excluded from scope.
agent_relevance: Separate measures can give opposite answers on the same manipulation. Report several signals and treat disagreement as information.

source: Scheiter et al. (2020) -- research agenda: resolution of effort appraisals
finding: The authors propose measuring the within-person correlation (resolution) between effort ratings and an objective effort measure, as done for confidence judgments, instead of comparing group means.
numbers: Resolution is usually computed over at least ten items per participant in metacognition work.
limits: A proposal, not a result.
agent_relevance: For the agent: check whether stated effort or confidence tracks token use per item, not only on average.

source: Schoor, Bannert and Brunken (2012) Role of dual task design when measuring cognitive load during multimedia learning
finding: The modality effect appeared in secondary-task reaction times only when the secondary task was spatially non-contiguous with the learning material. With a contiguous task (screen background color) there was no effect. Dual-task design choices can create or hide an effect.
numbers: N=96 (46 contiguous, 50 non-contiguous). Non-contiguous: visual-only RT M=916.19 (SD 564.57) vs audiovisual M=773.87 (SD 393.14), F(1,94)=20.17, p<.001, partial eta2=.17. Contiguous: M=526.87 vs 523.37, F=0.03, p=.87. Interaction F(1,94)=10.43, partial eta2=.10. Learning scores: no group difference (F=1.20, p=.28).
limits: One lab, one 13-minute program. Authors read the null as only partial use of working memory by the contiguous pair.
agent_relevance: A probe that is too easy shows nothing. Any side-task probe for the agent must tax the same resource.

source: Esmaeili Bijarsari (2021) A current view on dual-task paradigms and their limitations to capture cognitive load
finding: Dual-task methods lack standardisation. Studies adapt them case by case, with arbitrary choices of modality, frequency and timing. This harms validity and comparability, and the secondary task itself can intrude on the learning task.
numbers: Perspective article. No pooled numbers.
quote: a lack of validity and comparability between dual-task settings
limits: Opinion paper; no quantitative synthesis.
agent_relevance: Dual-task load probes are fragile and hard to compare. Do not build the agent around one.

source: Hu and Wang (2026) Effort as ceiling, not dial: reasoning budget does not modulate cognitive cost alignment between humans and large reasoning models
finding: Reasoning token counts of GPT-OSS models track human reaction times across tasks. Changing the effort setting (low, medium, high) did not change that alignment, and the effort setting only set an upper cap on tokens.
numbers: GPT-OSS-20B and 120B, 3 effort levels, 6 tasks. Within-task alignment rho .24 to .87 (20B) and .27 to .91 (120B), all p<.01. Mean alignment .570 / .567 / .562 for low / medium / high. Bayes factors BF10=.41, .43, .42 (inconclusive, lean null). Complexity contrasts: correct direction 16/16, 16/16, 15/16.
limits: Only 12 model-by-task units, so Bayes tests are weakly powered. Only GPT-OSS models. Human data come from an earlier paper. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Tokens are a usable load proxy, but the effort dial does not make the model think more in a human-like way. Token cost reflects training.

source: Hu and Wang (2026) -- cited background: alignment across training and skeptics
finding: Cited in the preprint: de Varda et al. found DeepSeek-R1 chain-of-thought length predicts human response time. Supervised fine-tuning distillation lowers the alignment. Vankov et al. (2026) found effort changes barely moved accuracy and traces were long even for trivial problems.
numbers: de Varda 2025: mean within-task rho=.57, across tasks r=.97 over seven tasks. Hu et al. 2026: teacher to distilled student rho .64 to .34. Vankov: negligible accuracy effect in 5 of 6 tasks.
limits: Second-hand numbers from the preprint's introduction.
agent_relevance: Alignment may be a trained property, not a free readout. Verify on our own models.

source: Davidson (2025) AI reasoning effort predicts human decision time in content moderation
finding: Chain-of-thought length of three frontier reasoning models predicts how long humans took to decide on the same pairs of posts. Both humans and models spent more when the posts were close in offensiveness.
numbers: Humans N=1854 (Prolific), 27,071 analysed pairs, mean decision time 15.3 s (median 11.4 s). One SD of CoT length goes with about 1 second more human time (Grok 4: beta=1.245, p<.001). Close pairs: humans +4.5 s (beta=4.532); models +1.06 SD (o3) to +1.15 SD (Gemini). Mean tokens: o3 303.3, Gemini 2.5 Pro 897.9, Grok 4 1600.3.
limits: Correlational. Synthetic posts, one task. Human time includes reading time. CoTs may be unfaithful.
agent_relevance: Tokens spent behave like a rough task-difficulty signal in a real task. Supports token count as the cheap load measure, but only a coarse one.

source: Davidson (2025) -- what the reasoning traces mention
finding: Reasoning traces mention contextual factors (replies, engagement, slurs) more often when posts are close, which hints that extra tokens do extra work in hard cases.
numbers: 200 Gemini traces coded by 3 raters: chi2=24.72, p<.001 and chi2=12.37, p<.001 for the two main contrasts; replies chi2=6.79, p<.01; engagement chi2=4.92, p<.05.
limits: Sample of 200 traces, one model. Trace text may not reflect actual computation.
agent_relevance: Trace content could be mined as a second load signal beside length.

source: Hughes et al. (2019) Cardiac measures of cognitive workload: a meta-analysis
finding: Abstract only. Several cardiac metrics are sensitive to workload manipulations (sample-weighted Cohen d). Heart rate variability responds to task load, event rate and task duration. Authors urge using several metrics.
numbers: No numbers read; abstract seen via OpenAlex.
limits: Abstract only; effect sizes not seen.
agent_relevance: Another sign that single physiological measures are fragile.

source: Usability-testing review (2026) Cognitive load measurement methods for usability testing: a critical analysis and framework (Human Factors)
finding: Abstract only. Systematic review of 87 experimental studies, 2001-2025. Most used: performance measures 19%, NASA-TLX 12%, eye fixations 11%. Proposes a framework to pick methods by interface type.
numbers: 87 studies; use shares 19% / 12% / 11%.
limits: Abstract only. Usage counts, not validity results.
agent_relevance: Performance is the most used load signal in practice, matching the plan to use accuracy.

source: Web search digest (2026) Human-user studies of LLM tools using NASA-TLX and EEG
finding: Search snippets said an EEG study of a prompt-formulation system found EEG and NASA-TLX did not correlate on raw values, which authors put down to EEG catching moment-to-moment load while TLX is retrospective. LLM tool studies use NASA-TLX on human users, not on models.
numbers: Not opened; no figures.
limits: Snippet only; source attribution to this arXiv id is from a search result list and is unverified.
agent_relevance: Almost all LLM work measures the human user's load. No standard measure of load inside an LLM was found.

source: Search digest (2026) Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning
finding: Snippet: on 160 best-explanation problems, averaging over several sampled reasoning paths strengthened the token-to-human-time link.
numbers: GPT-OSS-20B correlation rose from 0.41 to 0.55 when averaged (per snippet).
limits: Snippet only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Averaging several samples gives a cleaner load estimate than one run.

source: Baars et al. (2020) meta-analysis of effort and monitoring judgments (as cited by David et al. 2024)
finding: Earlier meta-analysis found that higher perceived effort goes with lower judged learning. David et al. 2024 re-ran this with a structural model and found the same sign but a smaller standardised path.
numbers: Baars 2020: r=-.35 effort vs monitoring. David 2024: beta=-.19 (full model) and -.22 (partial model, CI -.30 to -.13).
limits: Baars numbers are second-hand from David et al. Task type was a significant moderator in Baars but not in David.
agent_relevance: Effort-as-cue effect is moderate and shrinks under stricter modelling. Do not lean on self-reported effort.

source: Krieglstein et al. (2022) Systematic meta-analysis of the reliability and validity of subjective cognitive load questionnaires in experimental multimedia learning research -- scale points and domain moderators in detail
finding: Practical moderators: ICL reliability was highest with a 10-point scale and at least 7 points are advised; ECL did best with 5 or 9 points and in maths and logic material; GCL was highest with 11 points but fine on all but 7 points. The authors settle on a 9-point scale.
numbers: Subgroup contrasts judged by non-overlapping 95% CIs. Even-point scales (6, 10) gave lower ECL reliability.
limits: Moderator cells small; ICL and ECL advice partly conflict, so the 9-point choice is a compromise.
agent_relevance: If a rating is ever used, scale design matters little compared with the validity issues above.
